column1: # Shared block-dangerous cases, read by BOTH test-hooks.ps1 and test-hooks.sh.
# Why a table and not twin hand-written cases: two suites holding the same
# string do not test the same thing, they only look like they do. A case here
# is executed once per dialect against the dialect's own hook, so the two
# implementations are compared rather than the two test files.
# Format, tab-separated, four fields:
#   name <TAB> branch <TAB> expect <TAB> json
# Lines starting with '#' and blank lines are ignored. The json field is last
# because it is the only one that may contain spaces; it may not contain tabs.
# What may live here: only cases whose command is dialect-neutral and whose
# verdict means the same thing in both harnesses. PowerShell resolves the
# hook's output by parsing it; bash matches on substrings. Measured, they agree
# on 'deny', 'allow' and 'ask' for any syntactically valid single JSON
# statement, and on 'silent' whenever the hook emits exactly '{}'. They do NOT
# agree when it emits nothing at all: PowerShell reads empty or whitespace
# output as 'silent' while bash has no match for it, and a non-zero exit is
# 'error' in PowerShell against a separate fault path in bash. So a 'silent'
# case belongs here only once the hook's '{}' output has been measured on both
# sides, and 'notdeny' stays inline until that difference is closed.
# PowerShell-only syntax (Remove-Item, the call operator, `powershell
# -Command`) stays inline because it is not a shared command at all.
# The twin-coverage ratchet in test-hooks.sh counts these rows for both
# dialects. Adding a row here closes the gap by one; deleting one reopens it.
# name
git status is safe
git diff is safe
git add specific file is safe
git commit is safe

# Task launches (#280). A task is a second way to execute a command line, so
# the runInTerminal tiers have to hold here too. Four of these are worth
# reading twice: per the VS Code task docs, executable content reaches a task
# through four places, not one -- an os-specific scope overrides `command`,
# `options.shell` carries its own args, a single `command` string is passed to
# the shell verbatim so metacharacters survive, and substitution variables
# resolve where the classifier cannot see. An allowlist reading only `command`
# is decorative. `runOn: folderOpen` would execute later, outside any hook's
# view. Since #60 the tool is removed from every agent and denied outright, so
# every row expects deny -- including the reviewed-script rows that used to
# allow. Argument-bearing runs go through af-command's run_script; fixed ones
# through runTask.
# Most rows below name the tool `createAndRunTask`, which VS Code never sends
# (the real name is `create_and_run_task`, issue #74). They are kept because
# both hooks were measured to treat the two names identically, so the legacy
# spelling is a regression guard rather than a second code path.

# PowerShell literals (#581). The pipe-to-shell rule scans the whole line with
# quoted data removed, and it lexed every command as bash: a backtick counted as
# command substitution and here-strings were unknown. In PowerShell a backtick
# is an escape and @'...'@ / @"..."@ are literals, so a regex alternation or a
# Markdown table cell inside one was hard-denied. Real pipes must stay denied.
a PowerShell regex alternation with a backtick escape is data
a PowerShell single-quoted regex alternation is data
a single-quoted here-string with an apostrophe and a table cell is data
a double-quoted here-string with an apostrophe and a table cell is data
an escaped quote does not end a PowerShell string

bash: a backtick substitution piping to sh is still denied
